claim: Mutations in the AP2 complex alpha and mu subunits in C. elegans (encoded by the apa-2 and apm-2 genes) result in animals with pleiotropic phenotypes including reduced body length (Dpy), egg-laying defects (Egl) and uncoordinated locomotion (Unc).
source: Mutations in the AP2 complex alpha and mu subunits in C. elegans (encoded by the apa-2 and apm-2 genes) result in animals with pleiotropic phenotypes including reduced body length (Dpy), egg-laying defects (Egl) and uncoordinated locomotion (Unc).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gu et al., 2013) and by data presented in the manuscript showing phenotypes of mutants.

claim: AP2 complex alpha and mu subunit mutants exhibit a unique 'jowls' phenotype, in which the mutants exhibit bulges in the cuticle on either side of the head.
source: In addition, they exhibit a unique 'jowls' phenotype, in which the mutants exhibit bulges in the cuticle on either side of the head (Gu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation and by images in Figure 1A showing the jowls phenotype.

claim: Deletion of the sigma subunit (aps-2) produces a 'jowls' phenotype similar to alpha and mu subunit mutants.
source: Deletion of the sigma subunit (aps-2) produces a similar 'jowls' phenotype (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by images in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing the jowls phenotype in aps-2 mutants.

claim: The beta subunit is shared by both AP1 and AP2 in C. elegans and mutations in apb-1 are lethal.
source: while the beta subunit is shared by both AP1 and AP2 in C. elegans and mutations in apb-1 are lethal.
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on knowledge of the AP complex structure and function in C. elegans.

claim: A screen for mutants with the jowls phenotype identified multiple mutations in three genes coding for alpha adaptin, mu2 adaptin and the nematode homolog of FCHo.
source: We screened for mutants with the jowls phenotype and identified multiple mutations in three genes coding for alpha adaptin, mu2 adaptin and the nematode homolog of FCHo (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data from the genetic screen presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A deletion allele fcho-1(ox477) was generated by transposon excision.
source: We generated a deletion allele fcho-1(ox477) by transposon excision (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by the description of the molecular method and diagram in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All six mutant alleles of fcho-1 produced defects strikingly similar to mutants lacking AP2 subunits, including the 'jowls' phenotype.
source: all six mutant alleles of fcho-1 produced defects strikingly similar to mutants lacking AP2 subunits, including the 'jowls' phenotype (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by images in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing similar phenotypes.

claim: The similarity of fcho-1 and AP2 subunit mutant phenotypes suggests that AP2 function is compromised in the absence of FCHo.
source: suggesting that AP2 function is compromised in the absence of FCHo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypic similarity between fcho-1 and AP2 mutants.

claim: In C. elegans, the FCHO-1 protein is localized to the plasma membrane and binds to AP2 in a complex with Eps15 and intersectin.
source: In C. elegans, the FCHO-1 protein is localized to the plasma membrane and binds to AP2 in a complex with Eps15 and intersectin (Mayers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the wild type, AP2 is found in concentrated patches on the plasma membrane.
source: In the wild type, AP2 is found in concentrated patches on the plasma membrane (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1B.

claim: In fcho-1 mutants, AP2 is associated with the plasma membrane but does not form clusters.
source: In fcho-1 mutants, AP2 is associated with the plasma membrane (Figure 1C), but does not form clusters, consistent with previous reports (Henne et al., 2010; Cocucci et al., 2012; Mayers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data in Figure 1C and citations to prior work.

claim: The fluorescence signal of AP2 recovered approximately three times faster after bleaching in the absence of FCHo.
source: The fluorescence signal recovered approximately three times faster after bleaching in the absence of FCHo (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data in Figure 1C and 1D showing faster recovery in fcho-1 mutants.

claim: FCHo stabilizes patches of AP2 on the membrane and limits its mobility.
source: Thus, FCHo stabilizes patches of AP2 on the membrane and limits its mobility, consistent with previous studies (Henne et al., 2010; Cocucci et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from the FRAP data and is consistent with cited prior work.

claim: The artificial cargo CD4-GFP with a tyrosine cargo recognition motif accumulates on the cell surface in mutants lacking AP2 subunits and in fcho-1 mutants.
source: However, this cargo accumulates on the cell surface in mutants lacking AP2 subunits and in fcho-1 mutants, suggesting that AP2-dependent endocytosis is defective in fcho-1 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by cargo assay data in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: AP2-dependent endocytosis is defective in fcho-1 mutants.
source: suggesting that AP2-dependent endocytosis is defective in fcho-1 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an inference from the cargo accumulation data.

claim: The phenotype of fcho-1 mutants is not enhanced in double mutants with AP2 subunit mutations, indicating that FCHO-1 acts in the same pathway as AP2.
source: In addition the phenotype is not enhanced in double mutants indicating that FCHO-1 acts in the same pathway as AP2.
evidence: This is an inference from genetic epistasis analysis.

claim: A genetic screen for mutations that suppress a null mutation in fcho-1 identified 71 dominant mutations that confer increased fitness to fcho-1 mutants and suppressed the jowls phenotype.
source: We selected for suppressors that rapidly starved plates, and identified 71 dominant mutations that confer increased fitness to fcho-1 mutants and suppressed the jowls phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by data from the suppressor screen.

claim: All 71 suppressor mutations contained second site missense mutations in one of the four subunits of AP2.
source: All of these suppressed strains contained second site missense mutations in one of the four subunits of AP2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: None of the suppressor mutations exhibited loss-of-function phenotypes for the adaptin genes.
source: and none exhibited loss-of-function phenotypes for these adaptin genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The suppressor mutations all occur at conserved amino acids and cluster at sites likely to stabilize the closed (inactive) conformation when placed on the crystal structures of AP2.
source: These mutations all occur at conserved amino acids, and cluster at sites likely to stabilize the closed (inactive) conformation when placed on the crystal structures of AP2 (Figure 2A–C) (Collins et al., 2002; Kelly et al., 2008; Jackson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2A–C and citations to crystal structures.

claim: The suppressor mutations can be classified into four groups: (1) residues in the bowl-like interface between mu2 and other subunits, (2) residues stabilizing the N-terminus of beta insertion into sigma, (3) residues in the alpha helical solenoid, and (4) the phosphorylation site on mu2.
source: These mutations can be classified into four groups: (1) residues that lie in the bowl-like interface between the mu2 subunit and the other three subunits, (2) residues that stabilize the insertion of the N-terminus of the beta subunit into the cargo binding motif of sigma, (3) residues in the alpha subunit that are found in the helical solenoid that lies across the top of the complex, and (4) the phosphorylation site on the mu2 subunit.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the mutations mapped onto crystal structures.

claim: The suppressor mutations likely destabilize the closed conformation of AP2, suggesting that the open conformation of AP2 may bypass the requirement for FCHo.
source: It is likely that these mutations destabilize the closed conformation of AP2, suggesting that the open conformation of AP2 may bypass the requirement for FCHo.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural location of the mutations and their suppressor phenotype.

claim: These mutations would promote an open conformation of AP2, suggesting that AP2 may dwell in the closed state in the absence of FCHo.
source: In other words, these mutations would promote an open conformation of AP2, suggesting that AP2 may dwell in the closed state in the absence of FCHo.
evidence: This is an inference from the suppressor phenotype and structural analysis.

claim: A TEV cleavage site was inserted into a surface loop of the mu2 subunit to create a protease-sensitive version of AP2.
source: Because this poorly conserved region tolerates the insertion of various tags (Nesterov et al., 1999; Jackson et al., 2010), we inserted a TEV cleavage site in this sequence, and replaced the endogenous apm-2 gene with the protease-sensitive version of mu2 tagged with HA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the description of the molecular method and diagram in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and citations to prior work.

claim: After heat-shock induction of TEV protease, the level of full-length mu2 declined and a smaller 25kd N-terminal fragment accumulated over an 8 hr period.
source: After heat-shock induction of the protease, the level of the full-length subunit declined and a smaller 25kd N-terminal fragment accumulated over a 8 hr period (Figure 3B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The mu2 cleavage rate was slower in fcho-1 mutants even though the protease was induced to a similar level.
source: The mu2 cleavage rate was slower in fcho-1 mutants even though the protease was induced to a similar level (Figure 3B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: A larger fraction of AP2 is in the closed, protease-resistant state in fcho-1 mutants.
source: These data suggest that a larger fraction of AP2 is in the closed, protease-resistant state in fcho-1 mutants.
evidence: This is an inference from the slower cleavage rate in fcho-1 mutants.

claim: Two suppressors each for the alpha, beta and mu2 subunits led to an increase in mu2 cleavage in the double mutants compared to fcho(−) alone.
source: We tested two suppressors each for the alpha, beta and mu2 subunits, and each led to an increase in mu2 cleavage in the double mutants compared to fcho(−) alone (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by TEV protease assay data in Figure 4C.

claim: AP2 is in the closed conformation in the absence of FCHo and single amino acid changes in the complex are sufficient to tip the equilibrium toward the active conformation.
source: These data suggest that AP2 is in the closed conformation in the absence of FCHo and that single amino acid changes in the complex are sufficient to tip the equilibrium toward the active conformation.
evidence: This is an inference from the TEV protease assay data showing increased cleavage in suppressor mutants.

claim: The amount of rescue observed in the cargo assay was grossly correlated with protease sensitivity.
source: Indeed, the amount of rescue observed in the cargo assay (Figure 4B) was grossly correlated with protease sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing data in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: None of the suppressor mutations fully restored cargo endocytosis, even though all of the suppressors rescued growth and morphology.
source: However, none of these mutations fully restored cargo endocytosis, even though all of the suppressors rescued growth and morphology (Figure 4A and not shown).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Only the mutation that resulted in a profoundly protease–hypersensitive complex (μE306K) increased cargo internalization with high significance in fcho-1 mutants.
source: Only the mutation that resulted in a profoundly protease–hypersensitive complex (μE306K) increased cargo internalization with high significance in fcho-1 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Subtle conformational changes favoring active AP2 satisfied an organismal requirement for FCHO-1 without fully compensating for the endocytic defect of fcho-1 mutants.
source: These findings indicate that subtle conformational changes favoring active AP2 satisfied an organismal requirement for FCHO-1 without fully compensating for the endocytic defect of fcho-1 mutants.
evidence: This is an inference from the partial rescue of cargo endocytosis despite full rescue of growth and morphology.

claim: The vertebrate mu2 subunit is phosphorylated in a clathrin-dependent manner at threonine-156 by Adaptor-Associated Kinase (AAK1).
source: The vertebrate mu2 subunit is phosphorylated in a clathrin-dependent manner at threonine-156 by Adaptor-Associated Kinase (AAK1) (Pauloin and Thurieau, 1993; Conner and Schmid, 2002; Conner et al., 2003; Jackson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The phosphorylated core complex binds cargo motifs and phosphoinositides with higher affinity.
source: The phosphorylated core complex binds cargo motifs and phosphoinositides with higher affinity (Honing et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the fcho-1 suppressor screen, multiple mutations were isolated in the equivalent residue (T160) of the worm mu2 subunit, including a mutation to the phosphorylation-defective amino acid alanine.
source: In the fcho-1 suppressor screen we isolated multiple mutations in the equivalent residue (T160) of the worm mu2 subunit, including a mutation to the phosphorylation-defective amino acid alanine (Figure 4A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data from the suppressor screen in Figure 4A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Mutating T160 to the phosphomimetic residue glutamate also suppressed fcho-1 mutants.
source: Mutating this residue to the phosphomimetic residue glutamate also suppressed fcho-1 mutants (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: Cargo internalization was compromised in both the phosphorylation-defective and phosphomimetic mutants, consistent with previous reports.
source: Note that cargo internalization was compromised in both the phosphorylation-defective and phosphomimetic mutants (Figure 4B), which is consistent with previous reports (Olusanya et al., 2001; Semerdjieva et al., 2008; Jackson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4B and citations to prior work.

claim: The presence of a threonine at position 160 stabilizes the inactive state and any change to this residue is likely to destabilize the inactive state of AP2.
source: Our data suggest that the presence of a threonine at this position stabilizes the inactive state and that any change to this residue is likely to destabilize the inactive state of AP2.
evidence: This is an inference from the suppressor phenotype of both phospho-defective and phospho-mimetic mutations.

claim: AP2 is phosphorylated in the wild-type, and is hypo-phosphorylated in the fcho-1 mutant.
source: We found that AP2 is phosphorylated in the wild-type, and is hypo-phosphorylated in the fcho-1 mutant (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4D.

claim: All of the suppressor mutations tested increased phosphorylation relative to the fcho-1 mutants (except the T160 mutations themselves).
source: All of the suppressor mutations we tested increased phosphorylation relative to the fcho-1 mutants (except of course the T160 mutations themselves).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4D.

claim: Increased phosphorylation was associated with increased protease sensitivity of the mu2 subunit in the TEV assay.
source: Increased phosphorylation was also associated with increased protease sensitivity of the mu2 subunit in the TEV assay (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by comparing data in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: The open state is phosphorylated, and FCHO-1 is not absolutely required for phosphorylation, but rather AP2 in the active state is sufficient to induce phosphorylation.
source: These data demonstrate that the open state is phosphorylated, and that FCHO-1 is not absolutely required for phosphorylation, but rather AP2 in the active state is sufficient to induce phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference from the phosphorylation data in suppressor mutants.

claim: Threonine-160 is not completely exposed in the crystal structure of the open conformation, so it is unclear whether the side chain would be accessible to AAK1 in this state.
source: Nevertheless, this threonine residue is not completely exposed in the crystal structure of the open conformation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Jackson et al., 2010) so it is unclear whether the side chain would be accessible to AAK1 in this state.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure and citation to prior work.

claim: In the closed conformation β (E361) forms a salt bridge to μ (K411).
source: In the closed conformation β (E361) forms a salt bridge to μ (K411) (Figure 2A; Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2A, Figure 5A, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations in β (E361K) and μ (K411E) that break the salt bridge both suppressed the fcho-1 mutant phenotype.
source: We therefore analyzed mutations in β (E361K) and μ (K411E) that break this salt bridge, and found that both suppressed the fcho-1 mutant phenotype (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: The βE361K and μK411E mutations increased protease sensitivity relative to the fcho-1 mutant, and increased phosphorylation of threonine-160.
source: These mutations also increased protease sensitivity relative to the fcho-1 mutant, and increased phosphorylation of threonine-160 (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: Only the mutation that produced an acutely open complex (μK411E) significantly rescued the cargo-recycling defect of fcho-1 mutants.
source: Similar to previous results (Figure 4), only the mutation that produced an acutely open complex (μK411E) significantly rescued the cargo-recycling defect of fcho-1 mutants (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: The double mutant containing both the βE361K and μK411E mutations no longer suppressed the fcho-1 growth phenotype or cargo retrieval defect, and reversed the protease sensitivity of the single mutants.
source: The two mutations together no longer suppressed the fcho-1 growth phenotype or cargo retrieval defect of the fcho-1 mutants, and reversed the protease sensitivity of the single mutants.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B, 5C, and 5D.

claim: Phosphorylation of T160 in the double mutant was reduced relative to the μK411E single mutant but was not fully restored to fcho(−) levels.
source: Phosphorylation of T160 in the double mutant was reduced relative to the μK411E single mutant but was not fully restored to fcho(−) levels.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5E.

claim: The closed form as determined by crystallography predominates in the fcho-1 mutant and destabilizing the closed form can bypass the requirement for FCHO-1.
source: These results confirm that the closed form as determined by crystallography predominates in the fcho-1 mutant and that destabilizing the closed form can bypass the requirement for FCHO-1.
evidence: This is an inference from the salt bridge mutation experiments.

claim: FCHO-1 is composed of a membrane-binding F-BAR domain, a linker region, and a C-terminal μ-homology domain related to the medium subunit of AP2.
source: FCHO-1 is composed of a membrane-binding F-BAR domain (Henne et al., 2007), a linker region, and a C-terminal μ-homology domain related to the medium subunit of AP2 (Reider et al., 2009) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of FCHo protein structure and citations to prior work, and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The N-terminal F-BAR domain is dispensable for rescue of all fcho-1 phenotypes.
source: We found that the N-terminal F-BAR domain is dispensable for rescue of all fcho-1 phenotypes (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Constructs lacking the C-terminal μ-homology domain (μHD) failed to rescue cargo endocytosis, but increased the growth rate, protease sensitivity and phosphorylation of the mutants.
source: Constructs lacking the C-terminal μ-homology domain (μHD) failed to rescue cargo endocytosis, but increased the growth rate, protease sensitivity and phosphorylation of the mutants (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: Deletions that extend into the linker domain failed to rescue fcho-1 mutants.
source: However, deletions that extend into the linker domain failed to rescue fcho-1 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: The linker domain was previously found to bind the AP2 complex using pulldown assays.
source: The linker domain was previously found to bind the AP2 complex using pulldown assays (Umasankar et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The activation of AP2 by FCHO-1 could be via a direct interaction with the linker domain.
source: suggesting that the activation of AP2 by FCHO-1 observed here could be via a direct interaction.
evidence: This is an inference from the linker domain binding data.

claim: There is a small region of ∼90 amino acids in the linker domain that is shared with other FCHo homologs and the vertebrate protein SGIP1.
source: The linker domain of FCHO-1 is poorly conserved in general, but there is a small region of ∼90 amino acids that is shared with other FCHo homologs and the vertebrate protein SGIP1 (Figure 6A) (Reider et al., 2009; Uezu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 6A and citations to prior work.

claim: Expression of the ∼90 amino acid fragment alone was capable of rescuing fcho-1 mutants, including growth rate, endocytosis of cargo, and morphology.
source: Expression of this short fragment alone was capable of rescuing fcho-1 mutants, including growth rate, endocytosis of cargo, and morphology (Figure 6C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and not shown).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ∼90 amino acid fragment is sufficient to immobilize AP2 on the membrane in the photobleaching assay and to cluster AP2 into presumptive endocytic pits.
source: This fragment is also sufficient to immobilize AP2 on the membrane in the photobleaching assay and to cluster AP2 into presumptive endocytic pits (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The equivalent domains from mouse FCHo2, mouse SGIP1, and human FCHo1 also rescued fcho-1 mutants.
source: Moreover, the equivalent domains from mouse FCHo2, mouse SGIP1, and human FCHo1 also rescued fcho-1 mutants (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6C.

claim: The fragment from mouse FCHo1 rescued poorly.
source: though the fragment from mouse FCHo1 rescued poorly (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The small 90 amino acid region encompasses a large fraction of FCHO-1 function in vivo and is called the AP2 Activator motif (APA).
source: These results suggest that this small 90 amino acid region, called the AP2 Activator motif (APA), encompasses a large fraction of FCHO-1 function in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference from the rescue data.

claim: Silver-stained gels and Western blot analysis suggested the presence of all four AP2 subunits in the APA pulldowns from HEK293 cells.
source: Silver-stained gels (Figure 7A) and Western blot analysis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) suggested the presence of all four AP2 subunits in the pulldowns.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis of the pulldowns using MudPIT showed that the most abundant interacting partner for the APA domains from mouse FCHo2 and SGIP1 was the AP2 complex (∼10% of peptides).
source: The majority of the peptide reads were from the bait itself (Figure 7B), but the most abundant interacting partner for the APA domains from mouse FCHo2 and SGIP1 was the AP2 complex (∼10% of peptides, Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by MudPIT data in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: When the bait included the entire FCHo2 or SGIP1 proteins (or FCHo2 without the BAR domain), AP2 was still enriched; but additional components known to bind the μ-homology domain, such as Eps15, were also isolated.
source: When the bait included the entire FCHo2 or SGIP1 proteins (or FCHo2 without the BAR domain), AP2 was still enriched; but additional components known to bind the μ-homology domain, such as Eps15, were also isolated (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by MudPIT data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The interaction of the APA domain with AP2 likely occurs in vivo as well, since fluorescently tagged APA colocalizes with AP2 on the membrane in coelomocytes, and membrane association is lost in mutants lacking the mu2 subunit.
source: The interaction of the APA domain with AP2 likely occurs in vivo as well, since fluorescently tagged APA colocalizes with AP2 on the membrane in coelomocytes, and membrane association is lost in mutants lacking the mu2 subunit (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The interaction between the APA domain and the AP2 core is direct, as demonstrated using purified recombinant proteins in pulldown assays.
source: We demonstrated that the interaction between the APA domain and the AP2 core is direct using purified recombinant proteins in pulldown assays (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by pulldown data in Figure 7C.

claim: The APA domain does not appear to bind the appendages of the large adaptins, nor to the mu domain alone.
source: The APA domain does not appear to bind the appendages of the large adaptins, nor to the mu domain alone.
evidence: This is supported by pulldown data in Figure 7C.

claim: The APA domain bridges the AP2 complex since it binds both the alpha/sigma and beta/mu hemicomplexes.
source: Rather, it bridges the complex since the APA bait binds both the alpha/sigma and beta/mu hemicomplexes.
evidence: This is supported by pulldown data in Figure 7C.

claim: The APA domain in FCHo homologs from worms, mice and humans binds AP2 to destabilize the closed conformation and promote the active conformation.
source: Together these data suggest that the APA domain in FCHo homologs from worms, mice and humans binds AP2 to destabilize the closed conformation and promote the active conformation.
evidence: This is an inference from the binding data and rescue experiments.

claim: Mutations in the FCHo gene phenocopy loss of AP2 subunits in the nematode C. elegans, suggesting these proteins act in a single pathway.
source: Mutations in the FCHo gene were found to phenocopy loss of AP2 subunits in the nematode C. elegans, suggesting these proteins act in a single pathway.
evidence: This is an inference from the phenotypic similarity.

claim: FCHo acts upstream of AP2: the function of FCHo can be bypassed by constitutively open mutations in the AP2 complex.
source: We found that FCHo acts upstream of AP2: the function of FCHo can be bypassed by constitutively open mutations in the AP2 complex.
evidence: This is an inference from the suppressor screen results.

claim: The effect of FCHo on AP2 is direct: a 90 amino acid fragment of the linker domain in the FCHo family proteins binds AP2.
source: Moreover the effect of FCHo on AP2 is direct: a 90 amino acid fragment of the linker domain in the FCHo family proteins binds AP2.
evidence: This is supported by pulldown data showing direct binding.

claim: The activator fragment is necessary and sufficient for rescue when overexpressed in fcho-1 mutants.
source: This activator fragment is necessary and sufficient for rescue when overexpressed in fcho-1 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by rescue data in Figure 6.

claim: The AP2 complex associates with the plasma membrane with different lifetimes; some AP2 clusters are aborted rapidly (between 5–16 s) whereas others develop into fully committed pits (90 s).
source: The AP2 complex associates with the plasma membrane with different lifetimes; some AP2 clusters are aborted rapidly (between 5–16 s) whereas others develop into fully committed pits (90 s) (Loerke et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the absence of FCHo, the lifetime of AP2 at the membrane in cultured cells is quite brief (<10 s), whereas overexpression of FCHo stabilizes AP2 and promotes the growth of clathrin-coated pits with long lifespans (>25 s).
source: In the absence of FCHo, the lifetime of AP2 at the membrane in cultured cells is quite brief (<10 s), whereas overexpression of FCHo stabilizes AP2 and promotes the growth of clathrin-coated pits with long lifespans (>25 s) (Henne et al., 2010; Cocucci et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In fcho-1 mutant worms, the lifespan of AP2 on the membrane is reduced from 35 to 10 s.
source: Moreover, the dwell time of AP2 on the membrane is shorter; in fcho-1 mutants worms, the lifespan of AP2 on the membrane is reduced from 35 to 10 s.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data in Figure 1.

claim: The observations in fcho-1 mutant worms are strikingly similar to the observations of Cocucci et al (2012).
source: These results are strikingly similar to the observations of Cocucci et al (2012).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work.

claim: Previously it was thought that FCHo stabilizes AP2 on the membrane indirectly by binding Eps15 and intersectin, and these proteins in turn bind AP2 and stabilize the formation of a clathrin-coated pit.
source: Previously it was thought that FCHo stabilizes AP2 on the membrane indirectly by binding Eps15 and intersectin, and these proteins in turn bind AP2 and stabilize the formation of a clathrin-coated pit (Henne et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of a prior model supported by citation.

claim: The linker region of human FCHo1 was previously shown to interact with AP2.
source: The linker region of human FCHo1 was previously shown to interact with AP2 (Umasankar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The previous interaction between FCHo1 linker and AP2 was thought to be via the appendage domain of the alpha subunit of AP2, however the current study finds that the interior of the linker binds the core complex.
source: This interaction was thought to be via the appendage domain of the alpha subunit of AP2, however we find that the interior of the linker binds the core complex.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work and is supported by pulldown data in Figure 7C.

claim: The APA domain is conserved in metazoan orthologs of FCHO-1, but is absent in the yeast ortholog Syp1p.
source: It is curious to note that while the APA domain is conserved in metazoan orthologs of FCHO-1, it is absent in the yeast ortholog Syp1p (Reider et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and citation to prior work.

claim: Although the APA domain rescues fcho-1 mutants to grossly wild-type morphology and behavior, it does not fully rescue at a cellular level: endocytosis of cargo is not restored to wild-type levels by expression of the APA fragment.
source: Although the APA domain rescues fcho-1 mutants to grossly wild-type morphology and behavior, it does not fully rescue at a cellular level: endocytosis of cargo is not restored to wild-type levels by expression of the APA fragment.
evidence: This is supported by cargo assay data in Figure 6.

claim: Full rescue is only observed when the rescuing constructs include both the APA domain and the μ-homology domain.
source: Full rescue is only observed when the rescuing constructs include both the APA domain and the μ-homology domain.
evidence: This is supported by rescue data in Figure 6.

claim: The μ-homology domains of FCHo proteins bind Eps15 and Eps15-like proteins in pulldowns from HEK293 cells.
source: We have confirmed that the μ-homology domains of FCHo proteins bind Eps15 and Eps15-like proteins in pulldowns from HEK293 cells by extending the bait proteins to include this domain (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by MudPIT data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Binding of FCHo to Eps15 is likely required for endocytosis of cargo.
source: It is therefore likely that binding of FCHo to Eps15 is required for endocytosis of cargo.

claim: FCHo forms an independent complex with Eps15 and Intersectin and this complex functions in the recruitment of cargo to clathrin-coated pits.
source: It has been demonstrated that FCHo forms an independent complex with Eps15 and Intersectin and that this complex functions in the recruitment of cargo to clathrin-coated pits (Mayers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The F-BAR domain binds membrane and is required to recruit FCHo to the cell surface in both yeast and tissue culture cells.
source: The F-BAR domain binds membrane and is required to recruit FCHo to the cell surface in both yeast and tissue culture cells (Reider et al., 2009; Stimpson et al., 2009; Henne et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neither the F-BAR domain of FCHO-1 or the membrane association domain of SGIP are required for rescue of fcho-1 mutants.
source: By contrast, neither the F-BAR domain of FCHO-1 or the membrane association domain of SGIP are required for rescue of fcho-1 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by rescue data in Figure 6.

claim: The dispensable nature of the F-BAR domain conflicts with models in which this domain must bend the membrane for clathrin-coated pit formation.
source: The dispensable nature of the F-BAR domain conflicts with models in which this domain must bend the membrane for clathrin-coated pit formation (Henne et al., 2010)
evidence: This is an inference from the rescue data and comparison to prior models.

claim: The most important feature of the F-BAR domain is its ability to localize the APA domain to the membrane.
source: and instead suggests that the most important feature of the F-BAR domain is its ability to localize the APA domain to the membrane.

claim: In C. elegans, the APA domain of FCHo can be recruited to the membrane via interactions with other proteins independent of the F-BAR domain.
source: Apparently in C. elegans, the APA domain of FCHo can be recruited to the membrane via interactions with other proteins independent of the F-BAR domain.
evidence: This is an inference from the rescue data showing APA alone can rescue.

claim: The presence of a membrane-binding motif in all FCHo and SGIP proteins demonstrates that membrane interactions are important and conserved.
source: Nevertheless, the presence of a membrane-binding motif in all FCHo and SGIP proteins demonstrate that membrane interactions are important and conserved.
evidence: This is an inference from the conservation of membrane-binding domains.

claim: The first crystal structure of the AP2 core complex revealed that the binding pockets for cargo and membrane were partially occluded, representing a closed, inactive conformation of AP2.
source: The first crystal structure of the core complex revealed that the binding pockets for cargo and membrane were partially occluded (Collins et al., 2002). This structure was proposed to represent a closed, inactive conformation of AP2.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: Cocrystallization with cargo peptides led to partially open or fully open conformations of AP2.
source: Cocrystallization with cargo peptides led to partially open or fully open conformations (Kelly et al., 2008; Jackson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural work.

claim: The open conformation places the cargo- and membrane-binding pockets in coplanar face of the complex and is therefore thought to be the active form of AP2.
source: The open conformation places the cargo- and membrane-binding pockets in coplanar face of the complex and is therefore thought to be the active form of AP2.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge and inference from crystal structures.

claim: The gain-of-function mutations in AP2 that bypass the requirement for fcho-1 provide in vivo support for conformational changes in AP2.
source: The gain-of-function mutations in AP2 that bypass the requirement for fcho-1 provide in vivo support for these conformational changes.
evidence: This is an inference from the suppressor mutation data.

claim: The activated AP2 mutations that result in the most open (protease sensitive) and phosphorylated AP2 complex fully rescue the morphological and growth defects of the fcho-1 deletion.
source: The activated AP2 mutations that result in the most open (protease sensitive) and phosphorylated AP2 complex fully rescue the morphological and growth defects of the fcho-1 deletion.

source: It is likely that the activated AP2 mutations cannot recapitulate all of the normal functions of the AP2 complex, since it is known that FCHo has other functions beyond its actions on AP2, for example via interactions with Eps15 or Disabled-2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) (Reider et al., 2009; Henne et al., 2010; Uezu et al., 2011; Mulkearns and Cooper, 2012; Umasankar et al., 2012; Mayers et al., 2013).

claim: The activated AP2 mutants do not exhibit enhanced endocytosis or membrane association in an otherwise wild-type background.

source: It is possible that compensatory mechanisms counteract the open state of these AP2 mutants.

claim: The endocytosis assay may be at its detection limit because fluorescence from the artificial cargo is close to background levels in the wild-type.
source: Alternatively, our endocytosis assay may be at its detection limit because fluorescence from the artificial cargo is close to background levels in the wild-type.

claim: The formation of a closed form of AP2 is probably required to unbind membranes from newly endocytosed vesicles and to scan the membrane for new sites of endocytosis.
source: The formation of a closed form of AP2 is probably required to unbind membranes from newly endocytosed vesicles and to scan the membrane for new sites of endocytosis.
evidence: This is speculation about the function of the closed conformation.

claim: The coincidental presence of FCHo, cargo, and PIP2 can stabilize the open state, and the conformational changes in the complex then nucleate recruitment of clathrin and other pit components.
source: The coincidental presence of FCHo, cargo, and PIP2 can then stabilize the open state, and the conformational changes in the complex then nucleate recruitment of clathrin and other pit components (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) (Jackson et al., 2010; Kelly et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a model based on the data and citations to prior work.

claim: FCHo/SGIP class of proteins evolved to promote endocytosis by binding to, and stabilizing the open conformation of AP2.
source: We propose that the FCHo/SGIP class of proteins evolved to promote endocytosis by binding to, and stabilizing the open conformation of AP2.
